title: Vector forces and F = ma
what_it_asks: You are given several forces in $\mathbf{i}$-$\mathbf{j}$ form, sometimes with unknown constants, plus a mass or an acceleration. You add the forces to get the resultant, then use resultant force $= m\mathbf{a}$ in vector form. The result often feeds a magnitude, a direction, or vector suvat.
typical_structure: Most questions have one or two parts, sometimes three. A part is usually worth three to five marks, so a whole question is typically about eight marks. An early part often finds a resultant, an acceleration or an unknown constant. A later part then uses it to find a magnitude, an angle, a speed or a position, and it may say "hence". About a third of questions have a diagram.
mark_pattern: The most usual three-mark sequence is M1 A1 A1. The M1 is for adding the forces or setting the resultant equal to $m\mathbf{a}$. The two A1 marks are for the correct $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ components, or for two correct values. A four-mark part is often M1 A1 M1 A1, where a second method stage follows, such as a magnitude, an angle or a suvat equation. Sometimes it is M1 A1 dM1 A1, where the later method depends on the first. Longer parts repeat the M1 A1 pair for each stage. Two-mark parts are usually M1 A1. Accuracy marks make up most of the total, so a slip early on can spread along the chain.

where_marks_leak.text: Many students give an angle, speed or force to the wrong number of significant figures or decimal places. The final A1 is lost even though the method was right.
You treat $m\mathbf{a}$ as an extra force added to the others, or you get its direction wrong. The M1 for resultant force $= m\mathbf{a}$ goes, and the A1 marks and any dM1 after it go with it.
When finding the size of a force or a speed, you forget to square the components or to take the square root. The M1 for the magnitude is lost, and so is the A1 after it.
When a force triangle is drawn, you use the wrong rule or pair a side with an angle that is not opposite it. The M1 is lost, and the A1 marks that depend on it.
You round the resultant or an angle part-way through and carry the rounded value on. The final A1 can drift outside what is accepted.

write_to_earn: Write $\mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a}$ with the resultant on the left before substituting, so the M1 is secure.
Collect the $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ components separately and show each sum, so both A1 marks are visible.
Write the magnitude as $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ before evaluating it, and sketch the triangle before using $\tan$ for a direction.
Keep exact or unrounded values between stages, and round only in the final line to the accuracy asked.
On a show-that part, write the line just before the printed result and then the result itself.
check_before_you_leave: Angle measured from the stated direction?
